questions.stem: The concept of price elasticity of demand describes:
options: how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's price
how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in the good's price
how responsive the good's price is to a change in consumer incomes
how far the demand curve shifts when consumer tastes change
questions.explanation: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price. Responsiveness of quantity supplied is price elasticity of supply.

questions.stem: The price of a good rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 25%. Price elasticity of demand is:
options: 2.5, so demand is relatively elastic
0.4, so demand is relatively inelastic
2.5, so demand is relatively inelastic
0.4, so demand is relatively elastic
questions.explanation: PED = 25 / 10 = 2.5 (ignoring the negative sign). A value greater than 1 means quantity changes proportionally more than price, so demand is relatively elastic.

questions.stem: The price of petrol rises by 20% and quantity demanded falls by 4% in the short run. Demand is:
options: relatively inelastic, with a PED of 0.2
relatively elastic, with a PED of 5
unitary elastic, with a PED of 1
perfectly inelastic, with a PED of 0
questions.explanation: PED = 4 / 20 = 0.2, less than 1, so quantity responds proportionally less than price. Demand is perfectly inelastic only if quantity does not change at all.

questions.stem: Demand is unitary elastic when:
options: a change in price causes a smaller percentage change in quantity
a change in price causes an equal percentage change in quantity
a change in price causes no change at all in quantity demanded
any rise in price causes quantity demanded to fall to zero
questions.explanation: With unitary elasticity PED equals 1, so total revenue stays the same when price changes. No change in quantity is perfectly inelastic demand.

questions.stem: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is drawn as:
options: a horizontal line
a downward-sloping straight line
an upward-sloping straight line
a vertical line
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded is the same at every price, so the curve is vertical and PED is zero. A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic.

questions.stem: A small wheat farmer can sell any amount at the world price but nothing above it. The demand curve facing the farmer is:
options: unitary elastic, drawn as a rectangular hyperbola
relatively inelastic, drawn as a steep line
perfectly elastic, drawn as a horizontal line
perfectly inelastic, drawn as a vertical line
questions.explanation: Because buyers can get identical wheat elsewhere at the world price, any price rise loses all sales, so demand is infinitely responsive. This is the case of a price taker in a highly competitive market.

questions.stem: Two demand curves pass through the same point. Curve A is much flatter than curve B. For a price rise from that point:
options: quantity demanded falls more along B, which is more elastic
quantity demanded falls more along A, which is more inelastic
quantity demanded falls by the same amount along both curves
quantity demanded falls more along A, which is more elastic
questions.explanation: From a common point, a flatter curve shows a larger change in quantity for the same price change, so it is more elastic there. A steep curve shows that quantity responds little to price.

questions.stem: Which factor tends to make demand for a good more price elastic?
options: It takes a tiny share of income
It is habit-forming
It has many close substitutes
It is a basic necessity
questions.explanation: When close substitutes exist, consumers can switch easily if the price rises. Necessities, items that take a small share of income and addictive goods tend to have inelastic demand.

questions.stem: Demand for cigarettes is relatively inelastic mainly because:
options: they have many close substitutes that smokers can switch to
they take a large share of every household's income
consumers have plenty of time to adjust to each price rise
they are addictive, so smokers keep buying when prices rise
questions.explanation: Addiction makes consumers less responsive to price, which is why tobacco excise raises large revenue while cutting consumption only modestly. Many substitutes and a large share of income make demand more elastic.

questions.stem: Why is demand for a particular brand of breakfast cereal more elastic than demand for breakfast cereal in general?
options: There are many close substitutes for one brand, but few for cereal as a whole
Breakfast cereal in general takes a much larger share of income than one brand
A single brand of cereal is more addictive than breakfast cereal in general
Consumers have less time to respond to the price of one brand of cereal
questions.explanation: If one brand's price rises, shoppers can switch to another brand; if all cereal prices rise, the substitutes, such as toast, are less close. Narrowly defined goods have more substitutes and more elastic demand.

questions.stem: Demand for new cars is more price elastic than demand for salt. Which factor best explains this?
options: Cars are a basic necessity while salt is a luxury
Salt is bought less often than a new car is bought
A car takes a far larger share of income than salt
Salt has many more close substitutes than cars do
questions.explanation: A price change on a costly item has a big effect on a household's budget, so buyers respond strongly. Salt takes a tiny share of income, so a price rise barely affects how much people buy.

questions.stem: When petrol prices rise sharply, quantity demanded falls only a little in the first month but falls much more over the following years. The best explanation is that:
options: over time consumers find substitutes, such as efficient cars and public transport
petrol becomes less addictive over time, so drivers begin to buy far less of it
petrol takes a smaller share of income in the long run than in the short run
the number of close substitutes for petrol falls the longer the price stays high
questions.explanation: Demand is more elastic over a longer time horizon because consumers have time to change habits and buy alternatives. In the short run most drivers must still commute, so demand is inelastic.

questions.stem: A cinema raises its ticket price and finds that total revenue falls. This shows demand for its tickets is:
options: unitary elastic
perfectly inelastic
relatively elastic
relatively inelastic
questions.explanation: If revenue falls when price rises, quantity must have fallen by a larger percentage than price, which means demand is elastic. With inelastic demand a price rise would increase revenue.

questions.stem: A business sells 1,000 units a week at $20. It raises the price to $25 and sales fall to 900 units. Total revenue and PED are:
options: revenue rises from $20,000 to $22,500; demand is relatively elastic
revenue is unchanged at $20,000; demand is unitary elastic
revenue rises from $20,000 to $22,500; demand is relatively inelastic
revenue falls from $20,000 to $18,000; demand is relatively elastic
questions.explanation: Revenue goes from 1,000 x $20 = $20,000 to 900 x $25 = $22,500. Price rose 25% and quantity fell 10%, so PED = 0.4, inelastic, which is why revenue rose.

questions.stem: A firm facing relatively elastic demand for its product wants to increase total revenue. It should:
options: raise its price, as total revenue always rises with price
keep its price fixed, as revenue cannot change with elastic demand
lower its price, as sales will rise by a larger percentage
raise its price, as sales will fall by a smaller percentage
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, a price cut raises quantity proportionally more, so total revenue rises. Raising the price would lose more in sales than it gains per unit.

questions.stem: A skincare company spends heavily on branding to convince customers its products are unique. In terms of elasticity, its main aim is to:
options: make supply of its products more elastic so it can lower costs
make demand perfectly elastic so it can sell any quantity
make demand for its products less elastic so it can raise prices
make demand for its products more elastic so it can raise prices
questions.explanation: Product differentiation reduces the number of close substitutes in consumers' minds, so demand becomes less sensitive to price. This gives the firm more pricing power.

questions.stem: An airline charges much higher fares for flights booked the day before departure than for flights booked months ahead. The most likely reason is that:
options: airline supply becomes perfectly elastic close to the departure date
early bookers have fewer substitutes than last-minute travellers
last-minute travellers, often on business, have less elastic demand
last-minute travellers have more elastic demand than early bookers
questions.explanation: Travellers who must fly at short notice have few alternatives, so they are less responsive to price. Charging them more, and discounting for price-sensitive leisure travellers, raises total revenue.

questions.stem: Governments often place excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco. In terms of elasticity, these goods are chosen partly because:
options: elastic demand means the tax raises a lot of revenue
inelastic supply means the tax is paid entirely by firms
perfectly elastic demand means consumption stops completely
inelastic demand means the tax raises a lot of revenue
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, quantity falls only a little after a tax-induced price rise, so revenue holds up. Most of the burden also falls on consumers.

questions.stem: The concept of price elasticity of supply describes:
options: how responsive price is to a change in production costs
how far the supply curve shifts when technology improves
how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price
how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price
questions.explanation: PES = percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price. A shift of the supply curve due to technology is a change in supply, not elasticity.

questions.stem: The price of avocados rises by 20% and quantity supplied rises by 30%. PES is:
options: 0.67, relatively inelastic
1.5, relatively inelastic
0.67, relatively elastic
1.5, relatively elastic
questions.explanation: PES = 30 / 20 = 1.5, greater than 1, so supply responds proportionally more than price. A value below 1 would be relatively inelastic.

questions.stem: The supply of original paintings by an artist who has died is:
options: unitary elastic
relatively elastic
perfectly inelastic
perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: No more paintings can be produced whatever the price, so quantity supplied is fixed and the supply curve is vertical. A horizontal supply curve would be perfectly elastic.

questions.stem: A perfectly elastic supply curve is horizontal. This means that:
options: quantity supplied falls as the price of the good rises
firms will supply any quantity at one price, and none below it
suppliers will supply one fixed quantity whatever the price is
quantity supplied changes by the same percentage as the price
questions.explanation: At the given price, firms are willing to supply unlimited amounts, so PES is infinite. A fixed quantity at any price is perfectly inelastic supply.

questions.stem: Any straight-line supply curve that starts from the origin has a PES of:
options: 1, unitary elastic
0, perfectly inelastic
infinity, perfectly elastic
less than 1, relatively inelastic
questions.explanation: Along such a line, quantity and price change in the same proportion, so the percentage changes are equal and PES equals 1 regardless of the slope.

questions.stem: Why is the supply of fresh strawberries relatively inelastic in the short run?
options: Strawberries take time to grow and spoil quickly, so they cannot be stored
Strawberries have many close substitutes in the market for fresh fruit
Strawberries take a large share of household income in most families
Strawberry growers can easily switch their land to other crops at any time
questions.explanation: A higher price cannot quickly increase output because crops take time to grow, and perishable goods cannot be held in stock. Substitutes and share of income affect demand, not supply.

questions.stem: A factory is operating at 60% of its capacity. If the price of its product rises, its supply is likely to be:
options: perfectly inelastic, because capacity cannot change
unitary elastic, because output rises in line with price
relatively elastic, because it can increase output quickly
relatively inelastic, because it has no spare machinery
questions.explanation: Excess capacity means extra output can be produced without new investment, so quantity supplied responds strongly to price. A factory at full capacity would have inelastic supply in the short run.

questions.stem: Supply of manufactured goods such as tinned food is usually more elastic than supply of fresh milk. The main reason is that tinned food:
options: is durable, so producers can hold stocks to release when prices rise
is perishable, so producers must sell it quickly whatever the price
has more close substitutes, so consumers can switch to other foods
takes a smaller share of consumers' incomes than fresh milk does
questions.explanation: Durable goods can be stored, so firms can add to or draw down inventories as prices change. Perishable goods must be sold quickly. Substitutes and income share are demand-side factors.

questions.stem: Building more housing in a city takes years, partly because builders and tradespeople are hard to attract from other regions. The housing supply is therefore:
options: inelastic, because of the time horizon and low factor mobility
elastic, because of the time horizon and high factor mobility
inelastic, because housing has many close substitutes for buyers
elastic, because housing is durable and can be stored by builders
questions.explanation: Supply responds slowly when production takes time and when labour and other resources cannot move easily between regions or uses. This is a key reason housing prices rise strongly when demand increases.

questions.stem: Why is supply usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run?
options: Goods become more perishable over time and must be sold quickly
Firms have time to expand capacity and new firms can enter
Consumers have time to find substitutes and reduce what they buy
Prices are fixed by government in the short run but not the long run
questions.explanation: Over time firms can build plant, hire and train workers and new producers can enter, so output can respond more fully to price. Consumers finding substitutes affects the elasticity of demand.

questions.stem: Demand for a toy rises sharply before Christmas. A toy maker with relatively elastic supply, compared with one with inelastic supply, is likely to:
options: see a larger rise in price and no change in the quantity it sells
be unable to change output, so its revenue is unaffected
increase output more and gain more sales from the higher demand
increase output less and gain fewer sales from the higher demand
questions.explanation: Firms with elastic supply can respond quickly to higher prices by producing more, capturing more of the extra demand. Inelastic supply means demand increases show up mainly as higher prices.

questions.stem: A business invests in flexible machinery that can switch quickly between products. This is likely to:
options: make its supply more elastic, so it can respond to price changes
make its supply less elastic, so its output becomes fixed
make demand for its products more elastic, so revenue falls
make demand for its products perfectly inelastic
questions.explanation: Greater factor mobility within the firm lets it shift resources towards products whose prices are rising. Elasticity of demand depends on consumers' responses, not the firm's equipment.

questions.stem: Demand for a good rises. In which case will the equilibrium price rise the most?
options: When supply is perfectly elastic
When supply is unitary elastic from the origin
When supply is relatively inelastic
When supply is relatively elastic
questions.explanation: With inelastic supply, firms cannot raise output much, so most of the extra demand is rationed by a higher price. With perfectly elastic supply, price does not change at all.

questions.stem: A government places a $1 tax on a good with perfectly inelastic demand. The effect on the market is most likely that:
options: price is unchanged and quantity sold falls sharply
price rises by $0.50 and quantity sold falls slightly
price falls by $1 and quantity sold rises a little
price rises by the full $1 and quantity is unchanged
questions.explanation: Consumers buy the same quantity whatever the price, so sellers can pass the whole tax on. With more elastic demand, quantity would fall and producers would bear part of the tax.

questions.stem: Which good is most likely to have relatively inelastic demand?
options: Designer clothing
Prescription medicine
A particular brand of soft drink
Overseas holidays
questions.explanation: Prescription medicine is a necessity with few substitutes, so buyers keep purchasing when the price rises. Branded soft drinks, holidays and designer clothing have substitutes or are luxuries.

questions.stem: Which statement about elasticity along a straight-line, downward-sloping demand curve is correct?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic at high prices and elastic at low ones
Demand is more elastic at high prices and less elastic at low prices
Demand is less elastic at high prices and more elastic at low prices
Demand has the same elasticity at every point along the curve
questions.explanation: At high prices a given price change is a small percentage of price but a large percentage of the small quantity, so PED is high. Constant slope does not mean constant elasticity.

questions.stem: Demand for a good is relatively inelastic when its PED is:
options: between 0 and 1
greater than 1
exactly 1
infinitely large
questions.explanation: A PED between 0 and 1 means quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price. Values above 1 are elastic, exactly 1 is unitary, and infinite elasticity is perfectly elastic.

questions.stem: A concert promoter sells 4,000 tickets at $100. When it cuts the price to $80, sales rise to 6,000. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Demand is relatively elastic, so the price cut lowered total revenue by $80,000
Demand is unitary elastic, so the price cut left total revenue unchanged
Demand is relatively elastic, so the price cut raised total revenue by $80,000
Demand is relatively inelastic, so the price cut lowered total revenue by $80,000
questions.explanation: Revenue rises from 4,000 x $100 = $400,000 to 6,000 x $80 = $480,000. Price fell 20% and quantity rose 50%, so PED = 2.5, elastic, which is why a price cut raised revenue.

questions.stem: A government sets a binding maximum price on rental housing, where supply is inelastic in the short run. Compared with a market where supply is elastic, the shortage caused in the short run is likely to be:
options: larger, because inelastic supply means landlords cut quantity supplied a lot
zero, because a maximum price cannot affect quantity supplied in any market
larger, because inelastic supply means demand becomes perfectly elastic
smaller, because inelastic supply means landlords cut quantity supplied little
questions.explanation: With inelastic supply in the short run, quantity supplied falls only a little when the price is held down, so the shortage is mainly due to higher quantity demanded. Over time, as supply becomes more elastic, the shortage tends to grow.
